title: Is Hell Real, and Is It Forever?
excerpt: The church has always confessed a final judgment, and it has never spoken with one voice about what hell is like or how long it lasts.
body:
Hardly anyone meets this question as a point of doctrine. It comes at a funeral, when the man in the casket never had any use for God and his daughter is sitting in the second row. It comes in a child's bedroom, the week after camp, when a ten-year-old can't sleep because of something a speaker said about fire. It comes from the skeptic who has read the Gospels more carefully than we assumed, and who wants to know how the Jesus of the Sermon on the Mount could also be the one who talked about people being thrown into outer darkness.

Bertrand Russell put that last objection as plainly as anyone has. In a lecture in London in 1927 he said, "I do not myself feel that any person who is really profoundly humane can believe in everlasting punishment." He counted it against Jesus that he believed in hell, and he argued that the doctrine had made the world crueler. Russell was not a careless man. Anyone who has sat through a certain kind of sermon knows what he was talking about.

The church has two bad habits here, and they pull in opposite directions. One is to talk about hell with a confidence and even a satisfaction that the Bible never shows. The other is to stop talking about it at all, out of embarrassment, and hope nobody asks. The first has frightened people away from God. The second leaves people alone with the question, and it quietly tells everyone who was ever badly wronged that nothing will finally be done about it.

## What the Church Has Always Confessed

Two questions are tangled together here, and they don't carry the same weight.

The first is whether there will be a final judgment. On this the church has spoken with one voice from the beginning. The Nicene Creed, which Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Christians all confess, says of Christ that "He shall come again, with glory, to judge the quick and the dead," the living and the dead. Judgment is part of the faith itself. Scripture says that "it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment" (Hebrews 9:27), and no reading of the New Testament can remove it.

We tend to hear that as a threat. Many people, in many centuries, have heard it as a promise. If you have lived a safe life, a God who judges may sound harsh. If your village was burned, or your child was taken, or the man who harmed you died honored and at peace, a God who shrugs is the unbearable thing. When Abraham pleaded for Sodom he asked, "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?" (Genesis 18:25). He meant it as an appeal. He was counting on God's justice to be better than his own.

The second question is what becomes of those who are finally lost: what hell is, and whether it lasts forever. Here the church has not spoken with one voice, and the disagreement is very old.

## What Jesus Said

Almost everything the New Testament says about hell comes from Jesus. The word usually translated "hell" is *Gehenna*, and of its twelve appearances in the New Testament, eleven are his. Paul never uses it. If we want to drop the subject, we will have to drop it against the one person in Scripture who wouldn't.

Gehenna was a real place. It is the Greek form of the Hebrew name for the Valley of Hinnom, on the south and west of Jerusalem, where kings of Judah had once burned children in sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31). By the time of Jesus the name had become a word for the place of final punishment. Preachers often say it was the city's burning rubbish dump. That explanation can't be traced earlier than a medieval commentator writing around 1200, and it has no ancient support. What the valley had was a memory of the worst thing Israel ever did.

Jesus describes the fate of the lost in pictures, and the pictures don't combine into a single scene. It is "the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels" (Matthew 25:41). It is also outer darkness. It is a place "where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched" (Mark 9:48), a line he takes from the last verse of Isaiah, where the worm and the fire are consuming corpses. It is being shut outside a feast. It is destruction: "fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell" (Matthew 10:28). Fire and darkness can't both be literal, and that has led some people to say it is all only imagery. But an image stands for something, and nobody uses pictures like these for something mild.

It matters who he said these things to. He didn't aim his warnings at the people his culture already counted as lost. Most of them were spoken to disciples and to the devout. The ones who hear "I never knew you; depart from me" are people who have just listed the religious work they did in his name (Matthew 7:22–23). In his picture of the last judgment, the condemned are astonished to be there. Hell on the lips of Jesus is not a weapon handed to the righteous for use on outsiders. It is a warning to the people sitting in the pews.

## Three Ways Christians Have Read the Texts

The first is eternal conscious punishment. This has been the view of most of the church through most of its history, in the East and the West alike. It rests on the plain sense of several texts. Jesus sets the two destinies side by side in one sentence: "these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life" (Matthew 25:46). The same word describes both, and if the life doesn't end, it is hard to see how the punishment does. Revelation says of those who worship the beast that "the smoke of their torment goes up forever and ever, and they have no rest, day or night" (Revelation 14:11). Defenders of this view answer the charge of disproportion in two ways. Sin against an infinitely good God, they say, is not a small thing made large by a harsh judge. And the lost are not people who repented and were refused. They are people who go on refusing, so that hell is the lasting shape of a will that would not have God.

The difficulty for this view is felt by its own defenders. God "desires all people to be saved" (1 Timothy 2:4), and yet on this account he holds in existence forever those who never will be. The promise that God will be "all in all" (1 Corinthians 15:28) has to be read alongside a suffering that never stops.

The second is conditional immortality, often called annihilationism. It holds that the lost are finally destroyed and cease to exist. Its defenders are not softening the Bible. They argue that they are reading its commonest words at face value. The usual New Testament language for the fate of the wicked is death, destruction and perishing. "The wages of sin is death" (Romans 6:23). Whoever believes will "not perish but have eternal life" (John 3:16). Only God has immortality in himself, they point out, and he gives it to those who are in Christ. On this reading "eternal punishment" is a punishment whose result is permanent, in the way Jude says that Sodom underwent "a punishment of eternal fire" (Jude 7), though Sodom is not still burning. The view has early roots, and it gained a serious hearing among evangelicals in the last century. Edward Fudge argued it at length in 1982, and John Stott said in 1988 that he held it, tentatively.

Its difficulty is the pair of texts already quoted. Matthew 25:46 gives the punishment and the life the same duration, and Revelation speaks of torment and of no rest.

The third is the hope that all will be restored. A minority of Christians have hoped that God's judgment, however terrible, is finally a healing one, and that in the end no one will be lost forever. They point to Paul: "as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive" (1 Corinthians 15:22), and God's purpose "to reconcile to himself all things" through the blood of the cross (Colossians 1:20). In the third century Origen taught a form of this. In the fourth, Gregory of Nyssa, one of the chief defenders of the Nicene faith, taught it too, and was never condemned for it.

Its difficulty is the heaviest of the three. Jesus spoke of a door that is shut and of a chasm that "none may cross" (Luke 16:26). His warnings have no visible exit in them, and the church as a whole has never affirmed that all will be saved. A person may hope for more than he has been told. But a teaching that turns that hope into a certainty, and then tells people the warnings need not trouble them, has stopped reading the pages it quotes.

## How the Argument Has Gone

The early centuries were less settled than later ones remembered. Origen's teaching spread widely enough that when Augustine came to write the last books of *The City of God* in the 420s, he had to argue the point with fellow believers. He did it with courtesy: "I must now, I see, enter the lists of amicable controversy with those tender-hearted Christians who decline to believe that any, or that all of those whom the infallibly just Judge may pronounce worthy of the punishment of hell, shall suffer eternally." He thought they were wrong and said so for chapters. He also called it an amicable controversy and called them Christians.

Augustine carried the West. In 553 Origen's teaching was condemned under the emperor Justinian, and from then on eternal punishment was the settled doctrine of Catholic and Orthodox Christianity. The creed that bears the name of Athanasius ends by saying that "they that have done evil" go "into everlasting fire." The Protestant confessions kept the same teaching. The Westminster Confession says the wicked "shall be cast into eternal torments."

Then the imagination went to work on the doctrine. Much of what people picture when they hear the word comes from medieval art and from Dante, not from the Bible, which says nothing about circles or pitchforks or a devil who reigns there. In Scripture the devil is hell's prisoner. In July 1741, at Enfield in Connecticut, Jonathan Edwards preached "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God," the most famous sermon in American history. He read it in a level voice from a manuscript. The preaching that followed in the next two centuries often kept his subject and lost his gravity, and hell became a tool for getting a response by the end of the service.

## What Is Settled and What Is Not

Some of this binds every Christian. Christ will judge the living and the dead. Human beings are answerable to God, and it is possible for a person to be finally lost. There is no salvation apart from what Christ has done. These belong to the faith the creeds confess, and a Christianity that removes them is preaching a different thing.

Between the first two views, eternal conscious punishment and conditional immortality, the question is of a second order. The weight of the tradition lies heavily with the first, and nobody should pretend otherwise. But Christians who confess every line of the creeds and hold Scripture as their authority have come to the second, by argument from the text. Churches and teachers differ over it, and this essay doesn't settle it.

The third is in a different position. As a hope, held with the warnings fully in view, it has had a place at the edge of the church since Gregory. As a doctrine, taught as the sure outcome, the church has generally refused it, and it can't be squared with the way Jesus spoke.

What none of the three permits is the thing we have most often done, which is to speak about the fate of a particular person. Scripture never gives us that knowledge. The Catholic Church names saints and has never declared that any individual is in hell. That restraint is right, and every preacher at every funeral should practice it.

We haven't. We have preached hell with something close to relish, about people we didn't like, and we have used it to control the frightened. We have told grieving families things we had no way of knowing. We have terrified children with pictures the Bible never drew. Then, ashamed of all that, many of us went silent, and in our silence told the victims of the world that their suffering would never be answered. Each of those is a failure to speak the way Jesus did. When he came in sight of the city that was about to reject him, "he wept over it" (Luke 19:41).

## If This Question Frightens You

Some readers come to this subject already afraid, and for them an argument is the wrong thing to hear first. If you lie awake wondering whether you are headed for hell, notice who it is that the warnings of Jesus are meant to wake. They are aimed at the comfortable and the sure. To the frightened he says something else. A dying criminal with no time left to mend anything asked only to be remembered, and was told, "today you will be with me in Paradise" (Luke 23:43). Paul writes, "There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus" (Romans 8:1).

And some come to it because someone has died. No one can tell you what passed between that person and God. The church doesn't know, and anyone who says he does is claiming more than Scripture gives him. What we are given is the character of the Judge, and Abraham's question is still the right one to ask him.

If you're grieving as you read this, you don't have to resolve any of it before you're allowed to pray. Bring the question to God in whatever words you have; the psalms give you permission. Bring it to a person too, a friend or a pastor who will sit with you. If you have started to wonder whether you want to go on living, reach out today: in the US, call or text 988 for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. This essay can't counsel you, but [Find Help](/help) has other lines you can call and a page for grief.

The Christian answer to hell was never mainly a theory about it. The one who warned of the outer darkness is the one over whose cross "there was darkness over the whole land" (Mark 15:33). Whatever it means to be cut off from God, the Gospels say that he went there, and that he went so that no one would have to.

The Judge of all the earth will do what is just. He is the same one who, while they were driving in the nails, said, "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do" (Luke 23:34).

*"Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?"* (Genesis 18:25)

*"For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life."* (John 3:16)
